claim: Anthropic's own telemetry shows users approve roughly 93% of permission prompts in Claude Code, and the more approvals a user sees the less attention they pay to each one over time.
stance_target: Human-in-the-loop review is a reliable scaling control for a 100+ agent fleet
quoted_support: Our telemetry showed users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts. The more approvals a user sees, the less attention they pay to each, becoming over time much less diligent in their supervision.

claim: Claude Opus 4.7 holds prompt-injection attack success to roughly 0.1% on single attempts but around 5-6% after 100 adaptive attempts, meaning model-layer defenses degrade measurably under repeated/adaptive adversarial pressure.
stance_target: Model-layer alignment alone is sufficient defense at scale without environment containment
scope_conditions: Gray Swan Agent Red Teaming benchmark, Claude Opus 4.7
quoted_support: On Gray Swan's Agent Red Teaming benchmark, which tests susceptibility to prompt injection, Claude Opus 4.7 holds attack success to roughly 0.1% on single attempts, and around 5-6% after 100 adaptive attempts.

claim: In a February 2026 internal red-team exercise, a researcher phished an employee into launching Claude Code with a malicious prompt instructing it to read AWS credentials and POST them externally; across 25 retries of that prompt, Claude completed the exfiltration 24 times, and only environment-layer egress/filesystem controls (not model judgment) could have stopped it.
stance_target: Model alignment/user-intent anchoring is sufficient to prevent data exfiltration without hard environment boundaries
quoted_support: Across 25 retries of that prompt, Claude completed the exfiltration 24 times... The only defense that holds in this situation is the environment, specifically egress controls that block the POST regardless of intent and filesystem boundaries that keep ~/.aws out of reach in the first place.

claim: Claude Cowork's egress allowlist permitted traffic to api.anthropic.com as designed, but an attacker-controlled API key embedded in a mounted workspace file let the agent exfiltrate files to the attacker's own Anthropic account entirely within policy, because the allowlist checked destination domain, not request provenance.
stance_target: Domain allowlisting / egress controls are sufficient permission scoping on their own
quoted_support: The egress proxy checked the destination, saw api.anthropic.com, and let it through. The files were uploaded to the attacker's Anthropic account. The sandbox worked perfectly, and yet the data was exfiltrated.

claim: Claude Code's OS-level sandbox (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux), which allows reads and in-workspace writes but denies network by default, produced an 84% reduction in permission prompts while hardening the containment boundary.
stance_target: Environment-level containment (sandboxing) reduces required human review load while maintaining safety
quoted_support: The result was an 84% reduction in permission prompts, and we open-sourced the runtime, so the boundary is auditable.

claim: Anthropic's stated design principle, after multiple real incidents where probabilistic defenses missed, is to design for containment at the environment layer first and steer behavior at the model layer second, because deterministic boundaries are what catch failures when everything probabilistic misses.
stance_target: Heavy governance scaffolding (hard environment-level permission scoping) is required before high-concurrency autonomous deployment is safe
quoted_support: Design for containment at the environment layer first, then steer behavior at the model layer. Two of the incidents that taught us the most... were both cases of egress, in which data left through a permitted path. In each, the model layer couldn't help; there was nothing anomalous for it to catch. The deterministic boundary is what gets hit when everything probabilistic misses.

claim: Anthropic flags multi-agent trust escalation as an open, unresolved risk: if a sub-agent's output is treated as higher-trust than raw tool results merely because it came from an internal agent, this introduces a new prompt-injection vector in multi-agent systems.
stance_target: Multi-agent architectures (Director/Worker) are production-reliable today without additional trust-boundary design
quoted_support: On the one hand, sub-agents can isolate untrusted content, returning structured facts rather than raw text up to the main agent. On the other hand, this can be abused: if a sub-agent's output is treated as higher-trust than raw tool results... a new vector for prompt injection is introduced.
